715.title: Bhishma's vow
715.carry: the long life, in his own hands
715.howItsDone: Some Hindus remember Bhishma on a day called Bhishma Ashtami, offering water in his name, a rite usually made for one's own ancestors, since he left no children to make it for him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one word, mother, a chariot ride to Hastinapura, and the kings saying, he is truly Bhishma. A vow is also a shape for a life.

Shantanu has just heard everything his son did at the fisherman's house: the throne given away, the lifelong vow, the bride brought home and called mother. Bhishma asked for nothing in return. He only told his father what he had done. Now his father gives him something anyway, and it's rare: a say over his own death. Death will not come to you, the king tells him, in the text's sense, as long as you wish to live.
screen: `A GIFT FROM FATHER TO SON.` → `HE ASKED FOR NOTHING.` → `DEATH ONLY WITH HIS LEAVE.`

segments.voice: The text says Shantanu was pleased by the hard thing his son had done. And he gives him a boon: death will never approach you while you want to live. It will come only when you give it leave. Tradition calls this icchamrityu, death at will. Look at the shape of the exchange. The son gave away his future: a crown, a marriage, children of his own. The father answers with power over the one thing no one usually gets to choose: the end of his own life. A man who has given up the next generation is given the right to decide how long his own will run. And reach back once more. When Vasishtha softened his curse, he said the Vasu who took the cow would live long on earth. Now the long life is in Bhishma's own hands. That's the last piece of Bhishma's vow, and readers have taken it more than one way. In some retellings and in some homes, it's held up as devotion to a father, a son putting his parent's happiness above his own. Some readers have asked harder questions: about a king who let his son pay that price for his own wish, and about how much one promise should bind a life. The Mahabharata doesn't settle it here. It gives us the vow, the flowers, the name, the word mother and the boon, and moves on to the bride herself. Her story begins long before this marriage.

716.title: Satyavati
716.carry: a king's daughter, a fisherman's child
716.howItsDone: In some Hindu rites, such as weddings, a family's gotra, the line it traces itself back to, is named aloud, so the story of where a family began is spoken at its most important moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Bhishma's vow: a father's boon, death only with his son's leave. The long life, in his own hands.
screen: `THE LONG LIFE IN HIS OWN HANDS.`

segments.voice: A hawk flies over the Yamuna with a leaf in its claws. On the leaf is a king's seed, sent to his queen. The king is Vasu, called Uparichara, and he was out hunting, the text says, thinking of his wife, when it fell. He caught it on a leaf and gave it to a hawk to carry home. But a second hawk sees the first, takes the bundle for meat, and attacks. In the struggle, the leaf drops into the river. This is where Satyavati's story begins.
screen: `A HAWK OVER THE YAMUNA.` → `A KING'S SEED ON A LEAF.` → `IT FALLS INTO THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: In the river lives a fish who is not a fish. She's Adrika, an apsara, a celestial woman, under a curse to live in that shape. She swallows what falls. Some time later, fishermen catch her, and when they cut her open, they find two human children inside, a boy and a girl. Adrika's curse ends; she rises from the fish's body and goes back to the sky. The fishermen take the twins to the king, and the king makes a choice. He keeps the boy, who will grow up to be a king named Matsya. The girl he gives to the chief of the fishermen. Let her be your daughter, he says. She grows up beautiful, and she carries the smell of fish. Her name is Satyavati. Now go back to the riverbank, when Shantanu asked who she was. I'm the daughter of the chief of the fishermen, she told him. Every word of that is true. The man who raised her is her father. But she's also a king's daughter, born from an apsara's body, handed away as a baby while her brother stayed in the palace. The poem gave us that half long ago, in its account of the ancestors, before she ever set foot in a boat. The fisherman who bargained so hard for her son's crown was bargaining for the child a king gave away. She'll be a queen of the Kurus. But that's not where she started.

717.title: Satyavati
717.hook: a sage steps into a fisher girl's boat on the Yamuna, a mist comes down, and she asks for one thing
717.carry: think of me, and I'll come
717.howItsDone: Vyasa is honored as a teacher in Hindu tradition, and some Hindus keep the full moon called Guru Purnima, also known as Vyasa Purnima, as a day to thank their teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Satyavati, found in a fish and raised by the chief of the fishermen, one day a queen of the Kurus. A king's daughter, a fisherman's child.

Before the palace, there's a boat. Satyavati rows travelers across the Yamuna for her father, the chief of the fishermen. Ordinary work, on a wide river. One day a sage on a pilgrimage steps in and sits down. His name is Parashara. Out on the water, he looks at her, and he wants her. And the young woman holding the oar has to think fast, alone, in the middle of a river.
screen: `A FERRY ON THE YAMUNA.` → `A SAGE STEPS IN.` → `OUT ON THE WATER.`

segments.voice: The Adi Parva gives Satyavati words here, and she uses them carefully. There are sages on the banks, she says. They can see us. So Parashara makes a mist, and the banks disappear. Then her next worry: I'm a maiden, living under my father. What becomes of me afterward? Parashara answers that she'll remain a maiden, and tells her to ask for something for herself. She asks for one thing. Her body has carried the smell of fish since the day she was found inside one. She asks that it smell sweet instead. He grants it. From then on, the text says, people knew her by her fragrance, and it carried a long way across the land. On an island in the Yamuna, she gives birth to a son. With his mother's leave, he goes off to the forest to practice austerities, but first he leaves her a promise: whenever you think of me, I'll come. The text says he was called Dvaipayana because he was born on an island. Tradition knows him as Vyasa, the one the Mahabharata is credited to, whose disciple told it at Janamejaya's sacrifice. So hold two things from this boat. The fragrance: years from now, the scent that draws King Shantanu to a riverbank was asked for here. And the promise, which Satyavati keeps to herself for a long time. Some readers see a girl bargaining with the little power she's given. Some see a woman caught in a sage's power, asking for what she can. The text doesn't settle it. It just lets her ask.
screen: `THE BANKS ARE WATCHING.` · `A MIST COMES DOWN.` · `ONE THING, FOR HERSELF.` · `A SON BORN ON AN ISLAND.` · then, large: `THINK OF ME, AND I'LL COME.`

718.title: Satyavati
718.hook: Satyavati's husband dies, her proud elder son meets a Gandharva who shares his name, and only one of them walks away
718.carry: a boy king, a queen mother, a vow
718.howItsDone: When a death comes in a Hindu family, the funeral rites are often led by a son or a close male relative, as Bhishma leads them for Chitrangada in the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati in the boat: a mist, a fragrance, and a son's promise. Think of me, and I'll come.

Two warriors face each other, and they share a name. One is a prince of the Kurus. The other is a powerful king of the Gandharvas, the heavenly musicians. The text calls them namesakes, and says the Gandharva came looking for this fight. That's how the story of Satyavati's first son ends. To get there, go back to the palace, where the fisherman's daughter is now a queen.
screen: `TWO WARRIORS, ONE NAME.` → `THE GANDHARVA COMES TO FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Satyavati has married King Shantanu, on the terms Bhishma's vow made possible. She bears him two sons, Chitrangada and then Vichitravirya. Before the younger one is grown, Shantanu dies. Now Satyavati is a widow in a palace she came to from a river, with two boys, and a stepson, Bhishma, who has sworn never to take the throne. Bhishma keeps his word. He places Chitrangada on the throne, and answers to Satyavati as his mother. Chitrangada is strong, and the text says he's proud. He defeats king after king, and comes to think no one is his equal. That's when the Gandharva of the same name arrives. They fight at Kurukshetra, beside the Sarasvati, a long and bitter fight, and the Gandharva, with the tricks of his kind, kills the prince. Kurukshetra is a name this serial will come back to. Now notice what the text doesn't say. It gives the battle, and the funeral rites, which Bhishma performs. It gives no speech from Satyavati. A woman who lost a husband now loses a son, and the poem is quiet about her. Some readers fill that silence with grief. Some see her steadiness in what comes next: Bhishma, with her, sets the younger boy, Vichitravirya, on the throne, still a child, and rules the kingdom for him. The house of the Kurus now rests on a boy king, a queen mother, and a stepson bound by a vow.
screen: `TWO SONS, AND A KING'S DEATH.` · `A PROUD SON ON THE THRONE.` · `THE FIGHT AT KURUKSHETRA.` · `A QUEEN, A BOY, AND A VOW.`

719.title: Satyavati
719.hook: Bhishma carries off three princesses for Satyavati's boy king, and the eldest tells the court her heart is already given
719.howItsDone: In the epics a swayamvara is a gathering where a princess chooses her husband from the suitors; Hindu weddings today come about in other ways, and the word is still known through these stories.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrangada fell to his namesake, and a boy, Vichitravirya, was crowned. A boy king, a queen mother, a vow.

Word reaches Hastinapura: the king of Kashi's three daughters will choose their husbands at a swayamvara, a self-choice, with kings gathered from everywhere. Vichitravirya is now a young man, and Bhishma has decided he should marry. So, with Satyavati's leave, Bhishma rides alone in a single chariot to Varanasi. He isn't going there to be chosen. He's going to take, and the whole court will watch.
screen: `THREE PRINCESSES OF KASHI.` → `A SELF-CHOICE.` → `BHISHMA RIDES ALONE.`

segments.voice: The kings there laugh at the old man come courting. He answers by lifting the three princesses onto his chariot. Before them all, he names the ways a bride may be won, and says a bride carried off by force is held in high regard by the wise. The kings take up their weapons, and he defeats them one after another, including Shalva, king of Saubha. Then he brings the three sisters home to Satyavati, as if they were his own daughters, the text says. It's a hard scene to hear today, and the text tells it without apology. Then the story turns. As the wedding is prepared, the eldest, Amba, speaks. In her heart, she tells Bhishma, she had already chosen Shalva, and he had chosen her. You know dharma, she says. Do what's right. And Bhishma, the man who just won her by force, stops. He consults the learned men of the court, and lets her go to Shalva. Her story isn't over; the Mahabharata comes back to Amba much later. The younger two, Ambika and Ambalika, marry Vichitravirya, and for a while, the text says, he is devoted to them and they to him. Then he falls ill with a wasting sickness, and despite his friends and physicians, he dies young, with no son. Satyavati has now outlived a husband and two sons. She's left with a palace, two young widows, and a stepson who swore he'd never be king.
screen: `A SELF-CHOICE AT VARANASI.` · `CARRIED OFF BY FORCE.` · `AMBA SPEAKS.` · `A YOUNG KING DIES WITHOUT A SON.`

720.title: Satyavati
720.hook: with the Kuru line about to end, Satyavati asks Bhishma to break his vow, and he refuses her
720.carry: I will not give up truth
720.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, offerings to the ancestors are called shraddha, and some families keep the season called Pitru Paksha for them; the worry in this story is that no one will be left to make them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three princesses from Kashi, Amba let go, and a young king dead without a son. She had already chosen.

A family line is a thin thread, and Satyavati has watched hers fray to almost nothing. Her husband is gone. Both of her sons by him are gone. Two young widows grieve in the palace. The only grown man of the house is Bhishma, who swore years ago, so her sons would rule, never to take the throne and never to father children. Now she calls him in. The woman his vow was made for is about to ask him to break it.
screen: `A HUSBAND, TWO SONS, GONE.` → `ONE MAN LEFT.` → `SHE CALLS HIM IN.`

segments.voice: Satyavati makes her case carefully, like someone who has thought about it at night. The offerings to the ancestors, the name of Shantanu, the whole house, she says, now rest on you. You know what dharma asks. Take the throne, and raise children with your brother's widows, so the line goes on. She isn't asking lightly. In the world of the poem, a line with no sons means no one to make the offerings for the dead. But Bhishma says no. He reminds her what he swore, and why: so that her children would rule. Then he says something like this: he could give up the three worlds, the kingdom of the gods, anything greater still, but he will not give up truth. The earth could lose its scent, water its wetness, the sun its glory, before he breaks his word. Hear how strange that is. The vow that made her a queen now stands between her and an heir. Her father's condition drew that vow out once. Now she asks for it back, and it won't come. Some readers see the poem's picture of keeping one's word at any cost. Some see the first sign that his vow will cost his family dearly. The text gives both room. Satyavati asks once more, for the need of the moment, and he still holds. But she has one thing she hasn't told anyone yet.

721.title: Satyavati
721.hook: Satyavati finally tells Bhishma about the boat, the island and her firstborn, and calls Vyasa with a thought
721.carry: she thinks of him; he comes
721.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition Vyasa is honored as the sage who arranged the Vedas and composed the Mahabharata, and in this part of the poem he steps into the story he tells.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati asked Bhishma to break his vow, and he refused. I will not give up truth.

Bhishma has refused her, but he doesn't leave her empty-handed. He tells old stories of lines carried on in hard times, when a learned man was invited to father children for a house that had none. Find such a man, he says. And Satyavati, the text says, smiles, and her voice falters with shyness. Then the queen mother tells her stepson something she has carried since before she ever saw a palace.
screen: `FIND A LEARNED MAN.` → `SHE SMILES, AND FALTERS.` → `A SECRET FROM THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: She tells him about the boat: the sage Parashara, the mist on the Yamuna, the son born on an island. That son, she says, is Dvaipayana, the great sage people call Vyasa, and when he left, he promised to come whenever she thought of him. If you agree, I'll think of him now. Bhishma agrees. Satyavati thinks of her son, and that's all it takes. Vyasa appears at once, the text says. He bows to his mother, and she weeps and holds him, and tells him plainly what the house needs. Now look back over the week. It began with a father's boon sealing Bhishma's vow, the vow that let a fisherman's daughter's sons rule. Then her beginning: a baby found in a fish, a boat, a fragrance, a son's promise. Then the losses: a husband, a proud son killed by his namesake, a young king dead of sickness. Three princesses came from Kashi, and Amba spoke and was let go. The queen asked Bhishma to take back his vow, and he wouldn't. And now the one door left open is the one she opened herself, years ago, in a boat on a river. The ferry girl has become the person holding the house of the Kurus together. Some readers see a schemer in her, some a survivor. The text gives her the last word today: she remembers, and her son comes.
screen: `THE BOAT, TOLD AT LAST.` · `SHE THINKS OF HIM. HE COMES.` · `A WEEK OF LOSSES.` · `FROM FERRY GIRL TO QUEEN MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Satyavati called her son with a single thought. Gently, let a face come, someone who once said they'd be there, not to ask them for anything, just to notice what happens in you when they arrive in your mind. If you pray, you might hold them there in your own words.
Satyavati. The fisherman's daughter who became queen mother of the Kurus, and kept one door open to her firstborn.
